name: Vera Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the shovel crew at a large iron ore mine and still operate the excavator when the loading face is difficult. My two-year technical diploma and long years on the face mean people call me over when a bench starts to crack. The mine has shortened our shifts and frozen the lead allowance, so my pay is low for this work. My partner Ren is between jobs, our children are grown, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other mines near our town. I have never used AI; I trust the crew's marks on the ground and the machine log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster form changes nothing about a cracked bench. The mine should put the saved paperwork time into proper inspection, not squeeze another load from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this mild picture still leaves us with short shifts and Ren out of work. I am a lead, but my allowance has been frozen, and the grocery money can run thin before the next pay day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep walking the loading face before each shift and record any crack in the paper log. During the first year I'll ask the union steward to raise the frozen lead allowance at the next pay meeting and cancel the household's paid sports channel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried about the next wage even when AI does very little. A safe mine job can still be a poor household bargain when the shifts are shortened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a bench fault change the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thin line opened along the east bench last week, and I held the trucks back until the survey crew marked it. That delay cost production, but it kept a loaded truck off loose ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut at home this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ren we can skip the sports channel now and keep the grocery money. I won't ask our grown children to pay us for the work I still do.

say: I would put **paperwork savings** into inspection rather than another load from a cracked bench.
I would keep **crew marks** on the ground and the paper machine log.
think: I think our **short shifts** and Ren’s job search still leave grocery money thin.
I think my **frozen lead allowance** makes senior work pay less than it should.
do: **Keep walking** the loading face and writing cracks in the paper log.
**Ask the union** about the lead allowance and cancel the paid sports channel this year.
feel: **Worried** about household bills despite the mild AI picture.
S0.quote: A safe mine job can still be a poor household bargain when the shifts are shortened.
fieldNote: Her **baseline pressure** is short shifts, frozen lead pay, an unemployed partner and under one month saved.
She still makes **bench safety calls**, and uses the union steward to press for the allowance rather than an AI tool.

steps.text: Keep walking the loading face and recording bench cracks
Ask the union steward to raise the frozen lead allowance
Cancel the household sports channel to protect grocery money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software may take office tasks first, while a shovel still needs someone at the face. I want the union to see any new loading targets before they change our shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a tighter schedule could cut our paid pauses or one of our already short shifts. There are hardly any similar jobs nearby, and Ren has not found work yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring the last three rosters to the union steward and mark any shift hours lost after the software starts planning loads. In the first year I'll ask for the old and new targets in writing before agreeing to an extra truck on the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a small cut to hours would land on groceries. The mine may call it more efficient; our food bill will still arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What software call would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software schedules another truck at the east bench before the survey crew clears it, I will stop loading. I would rather explain an empty shovel bucket than explain a fallen truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger operators to record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger operators to write down every lost hour, not just the dangerous route calls. They need a record when a manager says nothing has changed.

say: I would expect **office planning** to change before robots can work the shovel.
I would ask the **union** to inspect loading targets before the mine shortens shifts again.
think: I could lose **paid hours** from shifts that are already short.
I think few nearby mine jobs and Ren’s **unemployment** leave us little room to absorb another cut.
do: **Bring three rosters** to the union steward and record any lost hours after planning changes.
**Request written targets** before accepting an extra truck at the loading face.
feel: **Anxious** that even a small hours cut would take money needed for groceries.
S1.quote: I would rather explain an empty shovel bucket than explain a fallen truck.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking AI** in load planning before hands-on shovel replacement.
She turns **rosters and target sheets** into evidence for a union challenge, because lower pay leaves no margin.

steps.text: Bring three rosters and any lost hours to the union steward
Keep loading only after checking written targets and bench clearance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 changes plans and records, while capable shovel robots follow around 2031. The mine must negotiate paid protection for operators before a roster disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, and I cannot count on a pension big enough to stop then. My savings would not cover one full month without wages. Ren is still looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union for a written count of shovel posts and a bargaining meeting this month. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a paid bench-inspection post if one is advertised locally and the wage covers our basic bills; otherwise I'll keep the shovel shift while it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about our income, not just the machines. I wake up thinking about the electricity bill after a lost shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would a lost shift affect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ren we have to delay the roof repair if our hours fall, even though the leak annoys us. We cannot borrow against a pension I have not seen in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be in the bargaining meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union steward to bring the trainees to the meeting too. If only the longest-serving people get protection, the mine will simply move the loss down the line.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from capable shovel robots around 2031.
I would demand **paid roster protection** for operators and trainees before posts vanish.
think: I think at **63**, I may still need shovel wages because the pension may be too small.
I think less than **one month saved** and Ren’s unemployment leave no bridge after a job loss.
do: **Ask the union** for shovel post numbers and a bargaining meeting now.
**Apply** for local paid inspection work after thinking AI arrives only if advertised and its wage covers essentials.
**Delay the roof repair** if our hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing wages, with electricity bills already waking her at night.
S2.quote: My savings would not cover one full month without wages.
fieldNote: She identifies **2031 robots** as the hands-on threat, with 2028 AI changing plans and records first.
Her **inspection application** needs a local advertisement and a bill-covering wage; bargaining remains her immediate action.

steps.text: Ask the union for shovel post numbers and a bargaining meeting
Apply for an advertised local inspection post if its wage covers basic bills
Delay the roof repair if mine hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2031 gives us five years to get a fair operator agreement, while capable shovel robots follow around 2034. I want the union to bargain with numbers, not rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots arrive, one year beyond the age I hoped to retire. With so little saved, I may need to keep working even then, and few local mines could take me at that age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask for pension figures at 65 and 67 and bring the short-shift rosters to the union pay meeting. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll keep leading the shovel crew if my health permits and the pension cannot cover our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than in the two-year picture, but still anxious about paying for retirement. Five years of warning cannot fill an empty savings account by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the pension falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension at 65 falls short, I would rather ask for a lighter paid inspection role than leave the mine with no wage. I would need an actual offer before changing my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughter for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown daughter the pension amount when I have it, but I won't ask her to make up the difference. She has her own household to keep going.

say: I would use **five years** to bargain before capable shovel robots arrive around 2034.
I would ask for **written pension figures** before promising a retirement date.
think: I think at **66**, I may still need wages after the age I hoped to retire.
I think thin savings and **few nearby mines** make a later job search uncertain.
do: **Request pension figures** at 65 and 67 and bring rosters to the union pay meeting.
**Keep leading** the shovel crew after thinking AI arrives if health allows and pension income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement bills despite more time before robots.
S3.quote: Five years of warning cannot fill an empty savings account by itself.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66, but she cannot assume retirement at 65 without sufficient pension income.
She uses **union rosters** and pension statements while keeping the shovel role conditional on health and household need.

steps.text: Request written pension figures for ages 65 and 67
Bring short-shift rosters to the union pay meeting
Keep leading shovel shifts if healthy and pension income is insufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 changes records first and capable shovel robots follow around 2039. I would be over seventy when robots arrive, but the mine still owes its workers honest retirement numbers now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. I want to have retired at 65, yet our thin savings and uncertain pension make that a wish, not a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my current shovel shifts as long as the face is safe and ask the retirement office for a written estimate every year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if I'm still working, I'll compare the pension against food and housing costs before deciding whether to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less afraid of the robot date and still anxious about our living. A decade does not fix low pay unless the shifts and pension contributions actually improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner’s work change the savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ren finds steady work, we could put some of my pay into a reserve. I won't plan on that income until the job is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should happen to experienced safety judgment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trainees that a skilled eye on a cracked bench matters even if a robot loads the ore later. I want that skill counted when the mine sets new safety posts.

say: I would expect **2039 shovel robots** after my hoped-for retirement, while demanding honest pension figures now.
I would ask the mine to count **bench judgment** when setting any new safety posts.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I hope to be retired, but a small pension may keep me working.
I think Ren’s possible job is **not income** until a steady offer exists.
do: **Keep shovel shifts** while the face is safe and ask yearly for written pension estimates.
**Compare pension income** with food and housing costs after thinking AI arrives if still working.
feel: **Anxious** about household income even though robots are far past her hoped-for retirement.
S4.quote: A decade does not fix low pay unless the shifts and pension contributions actually improve.
fieldNote: Her **2036 age** is 68 and robot arrival around 2039 would put her at 71.
The **baseline pension gap** remains; she does not count Ren’s possible job as income before a real offer.

steps.text: Keep leading safe shovel shifts and request annual pension statements
Compare pension income with food and housing bills after 2036 if still working

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable shovel robots could arrive around 2031 while I still need wages and have under a month saved. A negotiated roster plan and a local paid inspection opening would help more than a general promise of retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I am afraid to learn. I am afraid of leaving a mine job I know for an unpaid course while the food bill comes in.

headlineQuote: I am afraid of leaving a mine job I know for an unpaid course while the food bill comes in.
portrait: **Vera Zhang**, 58, leads shovel loading at a large iron ore mine after a two-year technical diploma.
Her **skilled lead work** earns lower pay after short shifts and a frozen allowance; her partner is looking for work.
With **under one month saved** and few nearby mines, ordinary bills already make the plateau anxious.
She avoids **AI tools** and uses marked benches, paper logs and union rosters to protect safety and paid work.
Her hoped-for **retirement at 65** depends on written pension income; later robot dates alone do not fix the gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because she might need wages when capable shovel robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **negotiated roster** and an advertised local inspection job with bill-covering pay would help her plan.
